conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/name: The Wars of the Three Kingdoms, the English Civil War and Cromwell in Ireland
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/religio: John Morrill famously argued that the English Civil War was 'not the first European revolution' but 'the last of the Wars of Religion': many who took up arms did so because they feared popery and Laudian 'innovation' or, on the other side, the destruction of the Church of England. Conrad Russell explained the breakdown through three interacting problems: religious division between and within the kingdoms, the strains of ruling multiple kingdoms, and royal financial weakness. Marxist historians such as Christopher Hill emphasised social and economic change, while others stress constitutional conflict over taxation and parliamentary rights. In Scotland the Covenant made religion the explicit cause; in Ireland confessional identity was bound up with land, colonisation and ethnicity. Religion was therefore a major cause, not the only one, and its weight varied between the three kingdoms.

conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/summary: A linked series of wars in Scotland, Ireland, England and Wales that began with Scottish resistance to Charles I's religious policies, included the Irish Catholic rising of 1641, the English Civil Wars, the execution of the king and the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland and Scotland. Preachers on every side cast the struggle as God's cause; the massacres of Protestant settlers in 1641 and of the garrisons and townspeople of Drogheda and Wexford in 1649 left lasting sectarian memories.
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/story:
Charles I ruled three kingdoms with three different religious settlements: an episcopal Church of England, a Church of Scotland with a strong Presbyterian tradition, and an Ireland whose majority remained Catholic under a Protestant established church and an expanding Protestant plantation. Under Archbishop William Laud the king promoted ceremonial worship, the 'beauty of holiness' and anti-Calvinist clergy, which Puritans regarded as a creeping return to popery. When a new Prayer Book was imposed on Scotland without consulting its General Assembly, its first reading in St Giles' Cathedral, Edinburgh, on 23 July 1637 provoked a riot. In February 1638 Scots of all ranks signed the National Covenant, pledging to defend the reformed religion, and in November the Glasgow Assembly abolished episcopacy.

Charles's attempts to coerce the Scots in the Bishops' Wars of 1639 and 1640 failed; a Scottish army defeated royal forces at Newburn and occupied Newcastle, forcing the king to summon what became the Long Parliament. Parliament impeached Laud and executed the king's Irish deputy, the Earl of Strafford, in 1641. In October 1641 Catholic Irish gentry in Ulster rose, fearing a militant Puritan Parliament and seeking to reverse plantation. The rising quickly became a popular attack on Protestant settlers: thousands were killed, including about a hundred men, women and children drowned at Portadown bridge, and many more died of exposure after being stripped and driven from their homes. Inflated reports in England spoke of 100,000 or more Protestants massacred; modern historians, working from the 1641 depositions, estimate several thousand killed directly. These reports convinced many English Protestants that a popish plot threatened them all.

Distrust over who should command an army to suppress the Irish rising brought matters to a head. After the king's failed attempt to arrest five members of the Commons in January 1642, both sides raised forces, and Charles raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642. The indecisive battle of Edgehill (October 1642) opened a war that divided counties, towns and families. In 1643 Parliament allied with the Scots in the Solemn League and Covenant, promising to reform religion in England and Ireland 'according to the word of God and the example of the best reformed churches', and summoned the Westminster Assembly of divines. Meanwhile the Irish Catholic leaders formed the Confederation of Kilkenny, whose oath pledged loyalty to the king and the free exercise of the Catholic religion.

The combined armies of Parliament and the Scots won at Marston Moor in July 1644. The reorganised New Model Army under Fairfax, with Cromwell commanding the cavalry, destroyed the king's main army at Naseby in June 1645; after the battle Parliamentarian soldiers killed or mutilated women in the Royalist baggage train, some of them believed to be Irish. In Scotland the Marquess of Montrose won a series of victories for the king with Irish and Highland troops in 1644–45, including the sack of Aberdeen, before his defeat at Philiphaugh, after which Covenanter troops massacred Irish prisoners and camp followers. Laud was beheaded in January 1645. In Ireland the papal nuncio Rinuccini pressed the Confederates to secure full Catholic establishment, and Owen Roe O'Neill defeated a Scottish army at Benburb in 1646, but quarrels over terms with the king divided the Confederation.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646 and was handed to Parliament, but his negotiations with the Scots provoked a Second Civil War in 1648, which Cromwell ended at Preston. Convinced that the king was a 'man of blood' who had defied God's verdict in battle, the army purged Parliament in December 1648, and Charles I was tried and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649. England became a republic, and the Church of England's bishops and Prayer Book had already been abolished.

In August 1649 Cromwell landed at Dublin. On 11 September his troops stormed Drogheda and, on his orders, killed the garrison of some 2,500–3,000 men together with Catholic clergy and an unknown number of civilians; Cromwell called it 'a righteous judgement of God upon these barbarous wretches' who had shed so much innocent blood in 1641. At Wexford in October soldiers ran out of control during negotiations and killed some 2,000 defenders and townspeople. Cromwell left Ireland in May 1650 after taking Clonmel at heavy cost, and his successors completed the conquest by 1653 amid famine, plague and guerrilla war. In Scotland, which had proclaimed Charles II king, Cromwell defeated the Covenanters at Dunbar in September 1650, after which thousands of prisoners died on a forced march and in captivity at Durham; Charles II's invasion of England ended at Worcester in September 1651.

The Cromwellian settlement confiscated most remaining Catholic-owned land in Ireland, transplanted many landowners west of the Shannon to Connacht and Clare, banished priests and sent thousands of Irish to the West Indies as bound labourers. The share of Irish land in Catholic hands fell from about three-fifths in 1641 to well under a quarter after the Restoration. Oliver Cromwell became Lord Protector in December 1653. Within England the wars had produced an explosion of religious sects, including Baptists, Fifth Monarchists and Quakers, but the monarchy and the episcopal Church of England were restored in 1660, and the Act of Uniformity of 1662 ejected nonconforming ministers.
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/nameOfG: Each side claimed God's favour. Royalists fought for 'God and the King' and the divine right of monarchs and defended the Church of England's bishops and Prayer Book. The Scots swore the National Covenant (1638) and, with Parliament, the Solemn League and Covenant (1643), binding nations to God by oath; Covenanter ministers preached that sparing enemies of the Lord was sin, and the cry 'Jesus and no quarter' was later associated with the massacre after Philiphaugh. Parliament held monthly fast days at which preachers such as Stephen Marshall, in his sermon 'Meroz Cursed' (1642), denounced neutrality as a curse from God. Cromwell read victories as 'providences' and 'dispensations' showing God's verdict, and the New Model Army marched singing psalms. The Irish Confederates' motto was 'Pro Deo, pro Rege, pro Patria Hibernia unanimis', and Rinuccini threatened excommunication against Catholics who accepted a truce with the Protestant royalists.
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/religio: Laudian ceremonialism and anti-Calvinist church policy convinced many English and Scottish Protestants that the king was leading the church back towards Rome.
The imposition of the Scottish Prayer Book in 1637 without the consent of the Kirk provoked the National Covenant and armed resistance.
Fear of a 'popish plot', intensified by Catholic influence at court around Queen Henrietta Maria and by reports from Ireland, shaped Parliamentary politics.
Irish Catholics sought freedom of worship and feared that a Puritan Parliament would suppress their religion completely.
Disagreement over whether to abolish episcopacy 'root and branch' split the English political nation in 1641–42.
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/otherCa: Charles I's financial expedients during the Personal Rule (1629–40), such as Ship Money, raised constitutional objections to taxation without Parliament.
The 'problem of multiple kingdoms' meant that policies made in London provoked resistance in Edinburgh and Dublin.
Plantation and confiscation of Irish land since the sixteenth century created deep ethnic and economic grievance.
Charles I's political inflexibility and distrust of his opponents made compromise difficult.
Local and factional rivalries, and fears for property and order, influenced many people's choice of side.

conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/casualt: Charles Carlton estimated about 190,000 deaths in England and Wales from fighting and war-related disease (some 3.7 per cent of the population) and about 60,000 in Scotland. Losses in Ireland, from fighting, massacre, famine and plague, were proportionally far higher: Sir William Petty's contemporary figure of over 600,000 is now considered too high, but modern historians such as Pádraig Lenihan still suggest the loss of perhaps 15–20 per cent of the population, roughly 200,000 or more. All figures are reconstructions with wide margins of error.
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/effects: Charles I was executed and England, Scotland and Ireland were united for the first time under a single republican government.
The Cromwellian conquest and land settlement transferred most Irish land to Protestant owners and laid foundations of the Protestant Ascendancy.
The monarchy and House of Lords were abolished and then restored in 1660, but the relationship between Crown and Parliament was permanently changed.
Ireland and Scotland suffered military occupation, and Ireland endured famine, plague and population loss.
Political ideas of popular sovereignty, religious liberty and the rights of 'freeborn Englishmen' emerged from Leveller and army debates.
Episcopacy and the Book of Common Prayer were abolished in England during the 1640s and restored, with the ejection of some 2,000 Puritan ministers, after 1660–62.
The Westminster Assembly produced the Westminster Confession, catechisms and Directory for Public Worship, which became the standards of Presbyterian churches worldwide.
Independent, Baptist and Quaker movements grew rapidly amid wartime freedom, creating a permanent English Nonconformity.
Irish Catholicism was driven underground, its clergy banished or killed, and Catholic identity in Ireland was fused with memory of dispossession.
Memories of 1641 and of Drogheda shaped Protestant and Catholic sectarian narratives in Ireland for centuries.
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/legacy: The wars remain contested ground. In England they are remembered as a struggle over Parliament and liberty; in Scotland through the Covenanting tradition; in Ireland through the twin memories of 1641 and Cromwell's 'curse'. Historians now read them as a 'British' crisis in which the religious divisions of three kingdoms collided, and the experience of godly warfare and its failure fed later arguments for religious toleration.
conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/dissent: Imprisoned at Derby in 1651, the Quaker founder refused an offer of a captaincy in the Commonwealth army, saying that he lived 'in the virtue of that life and power that took away the occasion of all wars'; the Quakers' 1661 declaration to Charles II made pacifism a mark of the movement.

A moderate royalist and friend of Christian humanists who longed for compromise, he was remembered by Clarendon as repeating 'Peace, peace' in his despair at the war before he was killed at Newbury in 1643.
The Digger leader rejected the use of the sword to establish God's kingdom, calling instead for the peaceful common cultivation of the land in 1649–50.
A Parliamentarian army chaplain who opposed the regicide and the army's later political actions; he later wrote of the bitter fruits of the war and worked for reconciliation among Protestants.

conflicts/wars-of-three-kingdoms/campaig: Oliver Cromwell and the New Model Army

Cromwell sailed from Milford Haven to Dublin in August 1649, stormed Drogheda and Wexford, took New Ross, failed before Waterford in winter, then captured Kilkenny and, at heavy cost, Clonmel before sailing home from Youghal in May 1650.
James Graham, Marquess of Montrose, and Alasdair Mac Colla

With Irish Confederate troops under Alasdair Mac Colla and Highland clansmen, Montrose won at Tippermuir, sacked Aberdeen, crushed the Campbells at Inverlochy and won at Auldearn, Alford and Kilsyth before being surprised and defeated at Philiphaugh in September 1645.
